utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Doctor, may I remind you of the affirmation you made, which still applies. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Schou. My name is Miroslav Vasic, attorney-at-law. I am about to start cross-examining you. Bearing in mind the Trial Chamber's instructions, I will be asking no questions in relation to the 18th, 19th or 20th of November, at least part of the 20th. My other learned friends will be dealing with those. I will be asking some other important questions. I hope that with the witness's assistance, we shall meet your expectations, Your Honours. Yesterday you told us you completed military academy and after that medical school, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In actual fact, you never ceased to be a soldier; you became a reserve officer of the Danish army and then you started practicing medicine. Would that seem to be correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to say which specific military schools you completed and when you became a specialist in all the fields that you told us about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to a military school where I became a officer in reserve, and it was in the infantry. In the infantry, when I became an officer, I was then connected to a battalion where I became an intelligence officer, and went to two small schools, I think about one week each.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These schools you have mentioned now, they had to do with your activity as an intelligence officer, I assume, didn't they? Or was it at this point in time that you were given a post as a reserve officer?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you explain the answer [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. There must be an error on the transcript on page 2, line 12. I said you were then assigned to work as an intelligence officer. What I want to know, whether those schools had to do with your activity as an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the last part of counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The school was only two weeks for the education for intelligence officer. And the school were -- where we had to learn about all this, you can say Russian tanks and vehicles, flights, boats and how they moved, how they normally arranged an attack, how they defend and all this kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You said that in 1991 you were with a group of Danish officers. And this group was given the task at -- or a mission to work as European Community Monitors. What I want to know, whether the rest of the Danish officers in that group were intelligence officers, too, or did they have other specialised fields of work in terms of their military duties?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all different kind of military people. There were men who specialised in -- in mines, there were men who were specialised in tanks, there were men who worked on airfield, and I think the rest of them were normally infantry soldiers, or officers, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You, however, were the only member of that group in permanent contact with the Danish foreign office. Would that seem to be correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were also in permanent contact with the Danish military commander and in 1991 he was based in Split, Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in contact with the Danish military in Denmark. I was also in contact with the -- the -- you can say the oldest officer of the Danish team, who was based in Split. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that for us, sir. Do you know what precisely the mission was of the Danish military team in Split back in 1991; in other words, what was their task?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their task were to monitoring the area of the coast. That's the only thing I know about their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they too part of the European Community Monitoring Mission or was this some sort of independent monitoring mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a part of the European Community Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can you tell us what precisely the remit was of the ECMM when you first arrived in the former Yugoslavia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it when I arrived or when the first Danish officers arrived?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume you might know about your own arrival and what the situation was at that point in time. So that's what I was asking. What were your tasks within the larger remit of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our task was to do what the head of mission -- the head of mission for the whole European monitoring mission, what he sent us to do, that was our task. And we were -- we were there all -- even if we were officers, we were all diplomats. We had diplomat card.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the task or the objective, if you like, was of the ECMM as a whole in the former Yugoslavia in 1991 at the time you joined?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the task were to monitoring the -- monitoring how -- what can you say, all activity between the different part in the conflict in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I imagine that there was a humanitarian aspect to the monitoring, that the objective was to keep the casualties down, or to keep any casualties from occurring at all?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You told us yesterday that the task you were assigned, before you had even left Denmark to join the ECMM, was to gather information on the military equipment of the JNA units, record all the numbers and features of JNA equipment, as well as list any equipment that you knew certain individual units of the JNA to be in possession of. Would that seem to be correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. We were told to watch all the equipment, the -- the army had, and the army, that's also of the Croatian army, because they have also cars we did not know, or tanks we did not know. It was the whole area we had to watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but is it not correct that you observed both equipment and units in the area?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We observed only equipment, not unit, because we were not -- we could not see any -- of course we could see the units, but we did not have any maps where they are situated at. We cannot say anything about them. We only think about the -- the equipment they -- they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This assignment to gather intelligence on military equipment was not given you by your superior command at Split. It was the Danish intelligence service that tasked you with this. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You knew at the time that any information you collected was bound to be classified information, military secrets, as they say, especially since there was an imminent danger of war in the area. You must have been aware of that, sir, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You also must have known that by collecting information that was classified and submitted -- and submitting such information to the intelligence service of your own country, you were guilty of the crime of espionage, which was defined as a crime under the existing laws in the former Yugoslavia and required the maximum punishment. Did you not know that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. There's something in the interpretation on page 5, line 24. I was asking if the witness was aware of the fact that he would thereby have been committing the crime of espionage. But we can agree that it was your mission and that you had no choice but to try and complete it, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not -- it was not the mission itself. The mission was to help the head of mission, of European Monitor Mission, with all their jobs. It was our mission. And then of course when we saw some of these cars we -- we look at them and sometimes took picture of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you did all these things under the auspices of the ECMM and you enjoyed a degree of immunity, as it were, based on the fact that this mission was accepted by all the parties and all the players in the former Yugoslavia at the time, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How exactly did you go about submitting any information collected to the intelligence service of the Danish army, and were the reports encrypted or open?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat. How exactly did you go about submitting such information to such military intelligence information to the intelligence service of the Danish army, and were the reports encrypted or unprotected, if you like?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no report back to the -- back to Denmark at this time. We only saw some cars and took some pictures of them and took them with us back, so when we work at home in Denmark, we could show that this was a T-72 when it could do like this. There were no crypted script or taking pictures and send them back. We just have our own pictures, and it was our own pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if other members of the regional centre, the ECMM regional centre, members of the ECMM regional centre in Zagreb had the same sort of task involving intelligence activity or spying, if you like, or were you the only one who was given a task of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know anything about the other countries' tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us within the mandate of the ECMM in the former Yugoslavia, were members of the mission allowed to pursue other work for their own country's military intelligence services at the expense of any other duties that they may have had?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would this not happen contrary to the spirit of the ECMM, such as you have described it for us?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether the ECMM head in Zagreb was familiar with your intelligence activity while you were a member of the mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to a different topic now. I want to know about the first time you arrived in the Vukovar area on the 19th of October, 1991. What exactly, verbatim, if you like, was the task you were given when you were first sent to the Vukovar area on the 19th of October?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task were to go with this convoy and to observe the, you can say, status of the hospital and to see how the evacuation were working out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You went there with other team members, but another person accompanying you was Major Mihajlovic, your JNA liaison officer, and he stayed with you throughout, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a liaison -- [microphone not activated]. We had a liaison officer, but I did not know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he stay with you throughout the duration of your mission on the 19th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my opinion, he do. Yes, he was with the convoy the whole way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something about the composition of your convoy. Did it contain any long trucks?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were one long trucks and some small trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was the composition of the convoy in keeping with the agreement that had been reached with the warring parties, or did the convoy also comprise a number of vehicles not previously agreed on? Do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was medical equipment being transported on that convoy as well as medicines for the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you really know what the vehicles on that convoy contained, or what they were carrying?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While testifying in chief, you explained how you reached the Bogdanovci area along an agreed route. You also explained how the local Croat commander at Bogdanovci derailed you, as it were, and sent you off on a farm track claiming that the surrounding area was booby-trapped. What I want to know is: Did you speak to this commander and ask him to remove these mines that were allegedly there?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not speak to him, and I did not know if our chief of the -- chief of this mission of his -- if he speak to the commander, I did not know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know at the time that the dirt track that you were forced to use was actually being used by the Croatian forces to bring in weapons and manpower as well as equipment into Vukovar, all the way up until mid-November 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about this change of route that you took from Bogdanovci to Vukovar, is this something that you informed the ECMM headquarters in Zagreb about?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the chief of the convoy contact Zagreb, but I know at that time we have very difficult with communication out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would that have been a proper procedure, so to speak? Whenever your team had to do something that strayed from your initial remit, you would have had to inform your headquarters about this, would you not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but it's up to the chief of this mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained how you reached the hospital on the 19th of October. You said that you saw the International Red Cross sign displayed on the roof of the hospital, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You remember that photograph from the set that was admitted as 338. You showed us the exact spot on the roof displaying a white area, but you said that the quality of the photograph was poor, and that was the reason you couldn't actually see the red cross there, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an -- I saw a red cross on the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What if I told you, sir, that we've had witnesses testifying here who were hospital employees at the time, and they said that there was no International Red Cross sign or symbol displayed on the roof of the hospital's main building at all? Would you still claim that you saw this Red Cross sign on the roof of the main hospital building with your very own eyes, and this is in reference to the 19th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the red cross on the roof on the 19th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified yesterday that you saw a Red Cross sign in the hospital courtyard on top of a lawn. Yesterday was the first time you ever talked about this. You never previously mentioned this in any of your statements to the OTP in 1995 or in your testimony before this Honourable Tribunal in a different case.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand that. It may be my error. The witness yesterday, from my recollection, said that the photographs that he had taken were a combination of November and October. Two of the photographs were October, I don't remember the Red Cross photograph being an October photograph, I remember it being a November photograph. I'm trying to find that. In relation to the question that is being put by my learned friend, saying that he -- that he has not mentioned this fact, at the end of the statement on page 7 of 9 and 8 of 9, there are references to photographs that were taken by this witness, and while I haven't had an opportunity of quickly checking the references, my understanding was that JAS 9 specifically says "20th of November, showing the side of Vukovar Hospital and the red cross on the roof." So there is specific reference to it in the statement. If that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this photograph that my learned friend has just referred to, as far as I can tell from the witness statement, this was taken in November, JAS 9. But my question was not in relation to the photograph of the hospital roof. I was asking about the Red Cross sign that he mentioned seeing in the courtyard on a lawn. I think he said that for the very first time yesterday. I wasn't asking about the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us whether you remember whether you have previously mentioned a Red Cross sign on the lawn of the hospital in any statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You testified in chief yesterday, you said -- and you said that in 1991, during your time at the hospital, you observed no military presence inside the hospital, but only around the hospital, within the compound. Do you perhaps remember seeing individual officers of the Croatian armed forces carrying pistols inside the hospital as well as members of the Crisis Staff, the Vukovar defence Crisis Staff, people who perhaps you met at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no person with weapon inside the hospital. I was guiding around in the hospital with a doctor from the hospital staff. And what the chief of this mission saw and what else happened in the hospital, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. When you testified in the Dokmanovic case on the 10th of February, 1998, did you not state as follows: For the benefit of my learned friend and the Chamber, it's 1292 of the transcript, paragraph 7 through 11. "[In English] ... inside hospital anyone, even one?" Answer: "Yes, I think we have negotiation, or talk with some of the leaders, and they were pistols, yes, inside the hospital in the basement." [Interpretation] Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember it. But if I said that at that time, I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You also testified in chief yesterday that during your stay at the hospital on the 19th of October you heard mortar fire near the hospital, the distance having been 30, 40, or perhaps 50 metres at the very most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This was actually mortar fire by the Croatian forces, the Croatian forces were opening fire from their mortars on JNA units. Would that not seem to be correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Upon your return, did you include any information on the fact that the Croatian forces were firing on the JNA from the hospital compound in any of your reports?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I reported it to the -- to the chief of this convoy, and it's also written in the paper from the chief to the head of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said yesterday that on your mission at the hospital on the 19th of October you were not placed in charge of the patients there, you were just monitors, and the patients were in the care of the Croatian side and Medecins sans Frontieres. Would that seem to be a fair assessment of what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained how you left Vukovar by the same route that you had taken to get there in the first place. What I want to know is who controlled the first stretch, as it were, of that village road on your way back to Bogdanovci. That's when the Croatian forces were accompanying you, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know who controlled the first street.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mean the village road? I was asking about the village road, not about a street.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I do not understand the answer -- the question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will repeat the question, thank you. You said that the convoy left Vukovar and took the same road that you had previously taken to get to Vukovar, the village road that the local commander of the Croatian forces from Bogdanovci had told you to use, and you had taken this road to get to Vukovar. What I want to know is: Under whose control was the initial stretch of that village road that led from Vukovar back to Bogdanovci?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that inside Vukovar, the road there, there were Croatian forces. But when we went to this small farmer road, I'm not sure that there were any people there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that at a certain point you were stopped because you came across a JNA tank. And that the vehicle with the Croatian soldiers at the head of the column turned into a cornfield and you said that you abandoned your vehicle. Why did you jump out of the vehicle? Were you not afraid that you would only raise suspicions as to who you were and what you were doing there? Wouldn't it have been better for you to have stayed in the vehicle [realtime transcript read in error "Vukovar"]?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I react as a soldier. If a tank is pointing at me, I want to get out of that car.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And correction for the transcript. Line 16 I said wouldn't it have been better for you to have stayed in the car, not in Vukovar. How far was the tank from you when you abandoned your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: About hundred metre.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was that the first tank that you saw during your mission in the area in such close proximity?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We saw tanks in those city we passed when we were -- when we are -- go to Vukovar. We saw tanks in every city. As I told yesterday, we passed no-man's land three times, I think, and at each side we saw tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the tank exhibit any sort of aggression or could you see whether they really intended to open fire by anything they may have done?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a kind of aggression that the -- the tank move its cannon in front -- to our car. That, I think, because we have no weapon, we were in a white car with a European community on, and after the car there was ambulance with red cross. So in that -- I think it was an aggression to point it at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the signs on your vehicles and the vehicle behind you? Weren't those safe guarantees that nothing would happen and that it was somewhat unrealistic of you to expect an attack as you were there as part of a humanitarian mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, we just jump out because we were soldiers. We were all four soldiers in the car and in that case we jump out. I think if we were civilian we would not jump out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understood. Thank you. You said that after that you were taken to an elevation. Was that actually the JNA front line, opposed to the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was the front line of the JNA forces. Because at that hill we also saw tanks and ordinary JNA soldiers cooking and something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And when you continued, when you left the elevation and went back to the main route, back to the agreed route, you said that perhaps after one or two kilometres the fourth vehicle in the column struck a mine; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The vehicle that you were in was in front of that vehicle; that is, the vehicle that struck a mine?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the front car and it was the truck and it was number four in the -- in this that hit the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you were all very alert, observing the road ahead, trying to spot any mines?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That was an asphalt road, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an asphalt road, but it was an asphalt road that had been used by forces, so there was a lot of dirt on the -- on the -- this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Therefore, looking out on to the road, you spotted no mines until the moment when that particular truck hit that mine; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Am I mistaken if I conclude that the mine that the truck struck wasn't actually on the road itself prior to the column passing, but rather that it was pushed under it and then the truck struck it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this as a soldier. I believe you have certain military education and training for an infantry officer; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you the following: If there is an asphalt road and you can't see a mine, and yet you were in the vehicle in front of the vehicle that struck the mine, can you offer any explanation as to how that mine got there, apart from it being pushed, so to speak, under that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say it -- it was pushed. I can only say that there was a mine on the road. How it came there, I did not know. When we went out, we saw mines on the road on some of these dirty things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would it be true if I said that you saw other mines after that truck had been struck, and at that time you saw mines that were ahead of you and not behind you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was between the number one and number two car we saw a mine in -- in the side of the road. Just -- just where the asphalt is stopped, and then in the side there, there was a mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you moved in the middle of the road; is that so?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That the first car move in the middle of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As for the other vehicles, I believe they followed in a column using the same track, being the safest way to move?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope they do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question as regards the convoy. Do you know where this convoy with the wounded was supposed to go to and where it finally ended? Was its destination Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know the destination Vinkovci, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were stopped at the elevation prior to going back to the asphalt road to Bogdanovci, do you remember whether a soldier of the JNA from one of the vehicles on the convoy asked for help, he wanted to be rescued, I believe his name was Ivan Zivkovic, because he was one of the wounded at the hospital. He was on the convoy, and the intention only could have been for him to be sent to Zagreb or to Vinkovci, as you say?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of this. This is the first time I've heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I asked you about that because the fact that he was crying for help is quite telling, because it points to the fact that there was no search of the vehicles at the elevation, as you suggested. Are you sure that there was a search conducted there indeed, or whether the search occurred at Marinci and when you -- that is when you were coming in, and when you were going out the search took place at Petrovci?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony in chief you stated, or rather you mentioned the convoy that departed from Vukovar on the 20th of November towards Sremska Mitrovica. I won't ask you about the initial stages of the travel; that's up to my colleagues to ask you about that. But I'm interested in the following: Would you agree with me if I told you that those seriously ill from the Vukovar Hospital were put on ambulances on the 20th of November, and that those who were lightly wounded were put on buses; and do you remember any ECMM report mentioning the figures of those seriously wounded put on ambulances and those of lightly wounded put on the buses? And I believe there should also be a number of the medical staff mentioned there of those who were taken to Sremska Mitrovica. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's two questions in one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I perhaps am pessimistic. Could I ask for them perhaps to be dealt with individually?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, thank you. I can split up the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the fact that in one of the reports of the ECMM the fact is mentioned that 84 seriously injured were put on ambulances and those slightly injured were put on the buses together with the medical staff on the 20th of November, 1991 to be transported from the Vukovar Hospital to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, that wasn't the first question. It's changed its form. Because the first question related to the question where it says: "If I told you that those seriously ill from the Vukovar Hospital were put on ambulances on the 20th." And the inference is quite clearly that there has been an element of care for those, namely all of them, to be put on ambulances. So I would ask my learned friend if in actual fact that is what he is suggesting, or whether it is a report that deals with numbers. And if it is a report, could the witness see the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could we please have 321 on the screen, page 3, the number being 0038-1419.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you have the tabs before you, that's tab 25. In English, that's also page 3. Sir, could you please look under b, teams Belgrade/Sarajevo. Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There is the Roman numeral (iii) that reads: "[In English] 1430 p.m., the team reported that: 82 wounded had been loaded on to 15 ambulances; b, 263 walking winded had been loaded into 5 buses; c, the convoy included 17 doctors, 6 nurses and 11 escort personnel." [Interpretation] Would you agree with me that this is what the report states?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, on this point, the way the question was put was that there was reference to seriously wounded being put on ambulances, the report. The report does not say that. And therefore it's an unfair question. So if my learned friend is going to quote from a report, I would be very grateful if he quoted it accurately. If you look at the question on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you can see the report. The subparagraph a. refers to 82 wounded and subparagraph b. to 263 walking wounded. Are you able, from that report, or from your recollection, to indicate whether the ambulances were used for serious wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ambulance were used for the first people that were evacuated from the hospital, and some of them were not serious wounded. And they just took them out of the hospital in a -- what do you call it, you go, you go, you go, there were no sorting of kind of injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you know that after the convoy departed on the 20th of November --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's easier for me when I can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The transcript, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have the English on the screen normally, so I can better understand when I can hear and see something. If I have the English here. I have it before, but now it's ... I had the same on the both screen. Before this picture came up, I had the -- some of the cases here, and I have your typing in English on this one, so I can hear and read what they are -- what the question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You want the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I presume it is all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I have only two or three other questions. Did you know that when the convoy left on the 20th of November another 110 patients left at the hospital in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Were left, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that some other wounded, other wounded are staying in the -- in the hospital and they were taken out the day after. Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know that a part of those wounded remained behind because they were supposed to go to Serbia, and the other part, that is 52 of them, had to wait for the 21st of November for the new ambulances to arrive because there was not enough room for them?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I were only aware that they had to wait because there were not ambulance enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what the ethnic make-up of those wounded who remained at the hospital was? What ethnic group did they belong to? Were they Serbs, Croats, Hungarians?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. Did you know that -- that an ECMM team spent the night between the 19th and the 20th of November in the area of the Ovcara cooperative or farm taking care of the civilian convoy that ended up there because the Croats wouldn't receive it on the highway towards Vinkovci and that convoy, the next morning on the 20th of November, moved towards Nustar and Vinkovci. Did you know whether one of your teams was there during the night and the next morning when they set off to Nustar?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your replies, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Borivoje Borovic, attorney-at-law. The first question I have for you: Did you complete a military college or military university, an academy, a full academy?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the terms you have here. But it was only a, you can call it, small school for reserve officers. It was not the normal military college where the -- the normal officers are going. It was another place, and only for reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the two weeks of your intelligence training and before you departed for Yugoslavia, did you learn what the officer ranks within the JNA were at the time, and could you share them with us?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not learn anything before -- before I go to Yugoslavia. I was -- the last three years before I went to Yugoslavia, I was just working in civilian hospital, and I was called out two days before I had arrived in Yugoslavia. And I was not volunteer, I was picked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you reached the town the Vukovar for the first time, were you able to distinguish between JNA ranks?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but only that I have learned some years ago before that the ranks of the Soviet Union, rank of the officers. I did not know the exact rank about it, if they have a different rank in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking from this chair today, do you know whether the ranks of the Soviet army were the same or different from those in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if they were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To conclude with this topic, one last question. Can you tell me what the rank of colonel looks like, what the insignia were at that time, or do you know it today?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time and today, I think a colonel had three big stars. Not the biggest one, the biggest one is for general, but three big stars. Bigger than the lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain to the Chamber in relation to the documents shown by Mr. Moore to you why did you sign them subsequently? You said that since you brought them, one -- that was one of the reasons why you signed them. Did you know that by signing subsequently you seriously jeopardised the authenticity of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's not right. That's a matter for the Judge to assess. It's wrong to put it to the witness that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can paraphrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony in chief, you stated that you subsequently signed the documents that you handed over to the OTP here; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct that I signed the paper I give to this Court, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you sign each page of that document? After 15 years, what was your reason?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the Court would know that this paper came from me. I had the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will leave it up to the Chamber as to whether that affects the authenticity of the documents that may be subsequently used in some other proceedings, hence I will conclude with this topic. My next question is this: In Hotel "I" in Zagreb, did you have direct communication with the Vukovar Hospital via phone?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not. If anyone else had, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 18th of November, 1991 did you know whether the regular telephone lines between Zagreb and your mission and the Vukovar Hospital was functioning?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you set off for Vukovar in November, before you departed did you know whether the Zagreb agreement in relation to Vukovar had been signed? Did you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the previous two days you stated that you went via Bogdanovci, and even a document was exhibited as regards that. Since you used the roads that you've already explained, when one goes from Bogdanovci to Vukovar, did you know whether the Croatian paramilitary forces blocked access routes to Vukovar from that direction?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me remind you of the statement you gave to the OTP investigators back in 1995. Can the usher please help me distribute copies? On page 3, paragraph 2 of that statement, the English reference is page 3, paragraph 3. Could you please just follow? I'll read it out to you. So if my reading is consistent, please confirm. "The only way we were allowed to travel from there was through Bogdanovci. It was impossible to use the shortest way, because Croats were afraid that if they removed the road blocks for the sake of the convoys the JNA would attempt to break through in those areas. From Bogdanovci on, we were forced to take a dirt track, an unsurfaced road through a cornfield all the way through to Lusac and Vukovar. We used the road recommended by the Croats and owing to that we did not cross any Serbian check-points." Was my reading correct, sir? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that I refreshed your memory by showing you this statement, do you now remember that the Croats did have road blocks and that the reason that you had to change your route was precisely what I have just read out to you? Wouldn't that seem to be the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- we were told that it was -- that this was the reason. I did not saw it. I did not see any. But of course -- when the Croatian forces, they said that they were afraid of this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for paragraph 3, that's seems to indicate that you were try to avoid all Serbian check-points. So my question to you is why? It's the last sentence that I have just read out. Why were you trying to avoid Serbian check-points?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have just passed one Serbian check-point in the city before, and now we have a Croatian point, and they could pass us through Vukovar Hospital. So I think that the chief of this mission decided that it was better to go this way. But -- it is his decision. I was not in the charge of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you know if in October 1991 your column was headed by a person named Branko Borkovic who was at the time the commander of the so-called ZNG? Is this something you were familiar with, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked by my learned friend, Mr. Vasic, a while ago about that tank appearing and you jumped out of the vehicle, and the reason you gave was all four of you were soldiers. Isn't that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Were you at this time wearing military uniforms or medical uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all wear white clothes, different kind of white clothes. Every country in the European Monitor Mission had their own white clothes, and we had only white clothes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then agree that at this point where you just jumped out of the vehicle and you ran for cover, you were there in your capacity as doctors, not as soldiers, given the clothes you were wearing and the roles you were playing on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there as EC monitor in white as we all -- we always were dressed in white.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we understand each other. Page 3, paragraph 1 of the statement that you have been given - in the English this is page 3, paragraph 2 - you stated, and you can follow, if you like, sir, just to check for consistency. There were paramilitary forces, Serbian forces, irregulars, and some volunteers, and the third group you described as Chetniks. I'm just paraphrasing, I'm not going into any detail here. But you did describe the third distinct group that you thought you could distinguish as Chetniks, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the name for them is, but we were told from the Croats that they were Chetniks, as same as you -- you told us that the other were Ustashas. And the Chetniks, they were not in a normal military uniform. They wear, you can say, part clothes you can buy in store to take on, who is -- look like military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you now know what the term means? What the term "Chetnik" means?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not still sure what this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. It wasn't me who told you that the other party were Ustashas. I'm not prone to advise anyone to use that sort of a term. But still let me ask you: Do you know how the term is used today, "Ustashas"?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were in Vukovar, you observed and toured both military and civilian facilities. Did you at any point in time learn that Croat paramilitaries were keeping their military and medical equipment and supplies in buildings such as the MUP, the municipality, the local recruitment office, the Eltz Palace, or any other such buildings and features? Did you have any information to indicate anything like that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will just correct you. I observed not military but only civilian facility in Vukovar. I only went to the hospital. And -- and I was not aware of the -- of course I could understand that in the town there is fighting. There must be some area where there must be military equipment, but we were not -- but I was not aware of where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how about a break now? I think that might be a good idea, since this seems to be the right time for it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. We will have a break now. Could I indicate, especially for the benefit of Mr. Lukic, that at the next break, because I have to meet some people, the break will probably be 35 minutes, and we will be able to extend beyond quarter to 2.00 to allow -- to make up for that lost time. We will adjourn now and resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I think it is now certain that in the Dokmanovic case, in your statement to the OTP and both when testifying in chief and being cross-examined, that there was mortar fire from somewhere around the hospital. That seems clear and perfectly certain now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It also follows from your statement that it was the Croats opening mortar fire near the hospital. What I would like to ask you now is: As a monitor, do you know about the fourth Geneva Convention dated 1949, what it says about protecting civilians in wartime? Do you know about Article 19, specifically, of this Convention, which talks about hospitals being used for military purposes, that if a hospital is used for military purposes it ceases to be a civilian facility. Did you have this sort of information while you were on your mission, and are you familiar with the fourth Geneva Convention that I have just referred to?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 19th of November, 1991, you returned to Vukovar. Was your only task to monitor the surrender of the Croats and the evacuation of the hospital, I mean either one of these or both?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was to monitoring the evacuation of the hospital. And it was -- it was my -- my mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When leaving Zagreb, did you know that the Croat paramilitaries were supposed to surrender at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday on page 6872, line 8, you said that when you arrived in Vukovar the northern section of Vukovar was still in the hands of the Croats. Could you please be so kind and describe in more detail what exactly you found when you got there?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of November I only went to the -- this hill outside the -- over the bus station, and at that moment we saw some -- or hear some fighting in the area 1, which is the area where the hospital is placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me take you up on that. You explained to my learned colleague yesterday about that photograph, there was a Danish monitor, and somebody that you yesterday defined as the town's defender. Just to avoid further confusion, the Trial Chamber stepped in, and you provided additional explanations about that photograph. My question to you is: While you were at that elevation, was your impression that that specific person was a member of any particular military unit? Just to give you a hand, you said that you were at this elevation overlooking the bus terminal and the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And that person, or all the person we saw in that, you can call it, military position, they were Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your impression that they were actually defending this area in the town in which you happened to be? And did they tell you anything to this effect?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the last they did not tell us anything. And if they were defending or trying to attack from that position, I don't know. They were on that position, and they were in the houses on that position, so if it's a defence position or an attack position, I -- that's not -- I can only think about. I have not spoken with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this was inside Vukovar, can you tell us why it was that yesterday you opted to use that precise phrasing "the town's defender," "one of the town's defenders" in relation to that specific person?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Why I used the word "defenders" is because you can call it the people are kind of local paramilitary, and they were -- I think it was, a local paramilitarian force. So if that's a defender or an attacker, I'm not -- I cannot tell you that. I can only -- because if he stay in that town, or live in that town, and this is his house, that's his -- is a defender. Because there is a war between the JNA and the Croatian. Not the JNA, sorry, between the Serb and the Croatian. So if he is the defender or some of the other are defenders, I can't tell you. It's not up to my position to say if this had to be taken by Croats or taken by the Serbs. It's depend on the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. In your report, this is Exhibit 340, I read the following: "The Croatian forces should lay down their arms before the evacuation begins." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your opinion was this something that was being requested by the JNA or is this based on an agreement? What do you know about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is based on my deciding when I was on that hill. I could see if we had to -- if we have any possible -- possibility to evacuate the hospital, the Croats had to lay down their weapons before we could reach the hospital at all. Because if there still would be Croatian force in that area, we would never reach the hospital. And that was our mission. It was to reach the hospital and evacuate the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then agree you were watching from that hill, and you realised that there was still fighting around the hospital which seemed to imply that the Croats had not yet laid down their arms, did it not?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had not laid down their weapons at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Likewise, in your statement to the OTP, your last statement, you should have it in front of you. On page 4, paragraph 6 of that statement, and the English reference is page 5, paragraph 1, you say that it had been planned to evacuate the hospital by using boats across the Danube two days before you even arrived. Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it not say there that the Red Cross should have been in charge of that particular operation?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It only said that the Red Cross planned to evacuate it. But I don't know if -- if they planned it alone or if we have the IC members with that, it was another than were -- that I hear about when I were in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which Red Cross did you have in mind when you wrote this? Do you know anything more about this operation that was planned? Whose boats would have been used to carry out the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know everything about the -- nothing about this thing. I just heard it on the conference in -- in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your statement also says that it was the Croatian forces that prevented the Red Cross from carrying out this evacuation by boats in the belief that they were actually JNA forces and not the International Red Cross. Is this something you heard about back in Zagreb or did you only learn about this upon your arrival in Vukovar? Did you know about this at all?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not wish to confuse you, because your answers seem very honest and clear to me. Nevertheless, in your statement on page 4 -- well, this is how it reads verbatim; you can follow. "The Red Cross planned to evacuate the hospital by using boats across the Danube two days before we arrived, but had to abort the operation due to the fact that Vukovar's defence believed that they were being attacked by the Serbs." Sir, this is a portion from your own statement. Does this jog your memory, do you remember that detail?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I not remember it, but I remember we had a meeting in -- in Zagreb where we were talking about this evacuation. That's the only thing I remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. Thank you. Was one of your objectives during the evacuation also to evacuate members of the Croat paramilitary forces known as the ZNG in a bid to shelter them from criminal prosecution for armed rebellion? What about this?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our mission -- or my mission were to evacuate the hospital and the members of the hospital, the staff of the hospital. And when I said "the hospital," I mean the wounded in the hospital and the hospital staff itself. There were no agreement about some other forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 19th of November, 1991 you were there in your capacity as an EC monitor. Did you know whether Croatia, at the time, was an internationally recognised country or state or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, with the utmost respect, how can this witness answer it when there's been so many questions about it in other areas?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He can speak, Mr. Moore, of his state of knowledge, will be understood by the Chamber as the state of knowledge of a person of his standing, experience and education, and not determining the legal issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, could I -- could I exchange the word for belief rather than knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I only say that I know that -- I think I know that Slovenia was accepted as an country, but I'm not sure at that time if Croatia was an accepted as a country or just that some other countries, I think U.S.A. and something, were preparing to accept Croatia. But I'm not sure -- I'm not sure of the status at that time. I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Since you were present in the area, perhaps you know whether that country had its own regular armed forces, irrespective of its international status, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that the Croatian had their own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what their uniforms looked like, their insignia, what sort of weapons did they have? The Croatian forces that, at the time, you recognised as such?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons they have, it were -- some of them were equal to their weapon they had in -- in the -- in the JNA -- in the Yugoslavian army. And some of them were -- I know were -- or I had heard had been brought in to Croatia from, I think, other countries. Not particular -- I can't mention any specific country. But I know that Croatia have weapons from the outside world, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Something else about this: While observing those Croatian forces, did you at any point in time realise that there was a variety of uniforms being worn? That is my first question. My second question: Were there some regular official, as it were, Croatian soldiers who weren't wearing any kind of uniform at all at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the first question, yes, they wear different kind of uniforms. To the second question, yes, I saw some civilian wearing arms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief that on the 19th of November an observer named Kypr spoke to the hospital director, Bosanac, using a mobile phone. We even have a statement you gave to the investigators confirming this. Yesterday on page 6886, line 17, you said this: "Dr. Vesna Bosanac spent about 13 seconds talking to Kypr, and all she said was something dreadful has happened." Isn't that what you heard, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have mentioned about 13 seconds or something. I only said that Mr. Kypr speak short with Dr. Bosanac, and she was telling that something -- awful thing was happening in the hospital. But, you know, it only what Kypr told me because I -- I cannot spoke Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The timing is not that important really, but you have just confirmed what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You know, I'm sorry. No. What is happening is that my learned friend, I'm sure inadvertently, is saying that a witness has said something, for example, at line 6886, Dr. Bosanac spent 13 seconds talking to Kypr, and all she said was something dreadful had happened. Line 17 does not say that. It says: "Yes, I can remember, she said that terrible things were going on and we had to come to the hospital immediately. Then the connection was broken." Now where does 13 seconds come from? There's been no evidence of 13 seconds, and how is this coming in in a question in such a particular way?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to quench my learned friend's curiosity. It was in the Dokmanovic case, page 1273, that the witness said this. But it's not about the 13 seconds. What matters is what Dr. Bosanac is reported to have said. "Something dreadful has happened." It may just be an unimportant bit of confusion. But can the witness now please go to his own statement to the OTP where he said: "That afternoon Petr Kypr talked to Dr. Bosanac on a mobile phone, and she told him that we should hurry to the hospital since the Serbs were expected to take the hospital very soon."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you stated this to the OTP. Do you stand by this previous statement that you made?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you help us out with this: How do you know that Kypr spoke to Dr. Bosanac, and how do you know what kind of phone he was using?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr said to me that he had spoken to Dr. Bosanac. And, I of course, had to believe him. And the only phone we had at that moment was a mobile phone, a car phone, so I can only say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you provide an explanation as to what Kypr had told you at the time and why you were asked to go to the hospital urgently before the JNA coming inside the hospital? Did he tell you something along those lines and did you do something about it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He tell me that he had spoken with Dr. Bosanac and that we had to go to the hospital because something bad was happened. Before -- and we had to go to the hospital before the Serb take over the hospital. And then he said that the connection was broken. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have Exhibit 338 put on the screen? This is a photograph number 0036-6987. I apologise. Just before that, could we please see Exhibit 170? Photograph 0053-1257A. I believe it comes second amongst the set of photographs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the help of the usher, could you please enter a mark in the place where you saw the Red Cross sign on the top of the building, and please mark that with 1.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which side of it, but it was either on the other side here. I can't remember from which side on we were staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put number 1 next to both of the circles.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was somewhere in the middle of the roof of the hospital, as you pointed out?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please draw the Red Cross sign that you saw on the lawn, could you enter a marking where you saw it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure if it was on this side or this side, but I think it was on this, or this at this place. I'm not sure which of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I told you that the side turned towards us represents the main entrance, the side with the main entrance, and that the other side was where the side entrance was, could you tell me whether you saw it in front of the main entrance or on the side where the evacuation exit was situated? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I cannot remember the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this as an exhibit, as marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be exhibit number [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see the previous photograph, Exhibit 338, the photograph 0036-6987. That's not the photograph of the hospital. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Could you see the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the photograph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind as to -- perhaps this is a bit more to the right compared to the place where you entered your markings before, but could you please mark the part of the roof where the white spot can be seen?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I meant, sorry to say, but I meant that we should try and zoom in on that part. Could you please erase the marking? Could we please zoom in on that part of the roof? More, please. Thank you. The question I have for the witness is the following: This part of the roof, for which you said bore the sign of the Red Cross, that underneath one can see the new planks used to patch up the roof. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me, you being an experienced military expert, that this was put on the roof after it was hit by shells, this what we can see here?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me then that the damage created by the shells carries over on to the area where the sign of the Red Cross was supposed to be, on both sides, and on the right in particular? I don't want to confuse you. Can you confirm for me the following: If a shell had hit that part of the roof, had there been the sign of the Red Cross there, do you think the white part would be as we can see here, or would that have been damaged heavily?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it would have been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't mean to suggest that this was put up on the 18th before you came, but would you allow for the possibility, based on what you can see, that this piece of cloth was put on the roof after the shelling, or perhaps you can't?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's -- I cannot say if it is put on after or before. No, I cannot. It's only -- I only take this picture because it's all Red Cross. So if were there before I came, or just put up the same day, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The last question in this line of questioning of mine, in your report, which is Exhibit 341, item A, you state the following, and you've expressed your views on it, in part. You have said that the leader of the Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand what Mr. Borovic said. Could that please be repeated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems the interpreters had some difficulty. I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You state that the leader or the head of the Red Cross was critical only of the JNA, that was under one; number two, that he did not compile a list of the wounded; and that under three, he did nothing. Did I read out your report correctly, a part of Exhibit 341?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you of the opinion today that the Red Cross, or rather its representative could have done much more in the given situation and that he was actually obliged to do that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean he -- I mean today that he could have done much more, but he was not able to do it because he was -- he said he was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know for certain how many people were evacuated from the Vukovar Hospital during your mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of the exact number of people. As also state in some of these papers I have seen, that we -- we were -- under the evacuation there was a lot of refugees who conjoined the -- the evacuation of the hospital. So how many wounded from the hospital itself, I'm not sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will allow for the third team to have more time at their disposal. This concludes my cross-examination. I would like to thank the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Borovic. Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Bulatovic, attorney-at-law, one of the counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin. Mr. Schou, before moving on to specifics, I wanted to clarify something. Based on your statement you gave to the OTP investigators, in that statement one can read that you completed your military training as a reserve officer with the rank of major; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a captain when I were in Croatia and then later I became a major, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's precisely what I wanted to ask, because I could see that during the mission you held the rank of captain. Could you explain to me what your status was within the monitoring mission, being one of its members? Namely, were you in any leadership position, were you a regular member, did you have any special authorisation or tasks?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that there was a lot of teams in this monitor mission, and I was not a part of one -- of -- of these teams. I was the only doctor in the ECMM, and I was under direct, you can say, command by the head of mission, and he told me what I had to do. And none of the other teams were able -- were -- were telling me what to do. It was only the head of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was the head of the mission that you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the mission was a Dutch ambassador, Van Houten, I think his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to being sent to the mission, did you undergo any training on how to behave as a member of such a mission, and, if so, where?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you before, I was working on the civilian job on Tuesday, and I was called by the military in Denmark and I went to the Croatia on -- I think it was Monday or Tuesday. And in -- in that meantime I -- it was only to equip me, and then we have one-hour talk with the Danish military intelligence. I have no training at all. I was just put in this mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how the teams were being formed, because you said there were many teams within the mission. Were they formed on an ad hoc basis to tackle any given particular situation, or was there any sort of a plan for the composition of teams?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my opinion, they were formed on ad hoc basis on every task. And it could be a Danish EC monitor who could be in charge of this team, and it could be a Dutch or a French or -- it depend -- it depend on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any such sort as plan of activities of -- or for the teams prior to being set off -- sent off to complete the task?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell what happened in -- in the headquarter in Zagreb. That's where I normally stay. And there it was which people were at home at that time the task came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When did you join the Belgrade mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the Belgrade mission on the -- I think it was the 17th, in the evening, or -- or 17th during the day. And I went to Belgrade together with the head of mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The 17th of which month? November?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who was your superior within the Belgrade mission?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- in Belgrade when I arrived there, I said I came with the head of mission, and of course he was the superior of all this mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a correction for the transcript. I don't think the witness's answer has been recorded on page 44, line 6. The witness said it was the 17th of November. I believe this should suffice to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say you went to Belgrade on the 17th of November, 1991 with the head of the mission. I'm interested in who was indeed the head of the mission who went to Belgrade with you on that date.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
